prompt: A dashboard shows a seven-day trailing average of orders. Black Friday falls on a Friday. Until which day does the spike keep the average high?

choices.text: Only on Black Friday itself
choices.why: That would be true of the raw series. An average carries the day for as long as it stays in the window.

choices.text: The following Thursday, six days after the spike entered the window
choices.why: Right. The spike sits in the window of the day itself and the six after it.

choices.text: From the Tuesday before to the Monday after, three days either side
choices.why: That is the centred average. A trailing window never looks forward.

choices.text: The following Sunday, when the week closes
choices.why: The window moves one day at a time; it does not reset at the end of a week.

prompt: An operations manager wants a line on the morning dashboard that updates as soon as yesterday closes. Which moving average fits?

choices.text: A trailing seven-day average
choices.why: Right. Only the past exists on a dashboard, and the price is a lag of a few days at a turn.

choices.text: A centred seven-day average, because it does not lag
choices.why: It does not lag, and it cannot be computed for the last three days, which are the ones the morning dashboard needs.

choices.text: A five-day average, since it reacts faster
choices.why: Five days hold a different mix of weekdays each time, so the weekly rhythm leaks into the line.

choices.text: A 2×7 average
choices.why: The 2×n trick is for centring an even window, and seven is odd.

prompt: Panela's data is monthly in a report. How many months long must a moving average be to remove the yearly season?
Somebody smooths Panela's daily orders with a five-day moving average and finds a slow wobble left in it. Why?

choices.text: Five is too short to remove any noise
choices.why: Five days do average noise away. What they cannot do is cancel a seven-day season.

choices.text: A trailing average always wobbles a little, whatever the length of its window
choices.why: A seven-day trailing average of the same data does not wobble weekly.

choices.text: The yearly season is leaking
choices.why: A yearly swing is far slower than a wobble that repeats every week or so.

choices.text: Five days are not a whole week
choices.why: Right. The window has to be the period for the season to cancel.

prompt: A Monday was 296 orders above a Saturday in 2023 and 445 in 2025, and about 36 per cent above in both years. What does that say?

choices.text: The season is additive, because the gap is in orders
choices.why: An additive season keeps the gap in orders fixed, and here it grew by half.

choices.text: The weekly season is getting stronger every year, so it will soon dominate the trend
choices.why: As a proportion it did not grow at all. The gap grew because the level grew.

choices.text: The season is multiplicative
choices.why: Right. A constant proportion and a growing gap is the multiplicative signature.

choices.text: Nothing, until a decomposition is run
choices.why: This is the test that chooses which decomposition to run.

prompt: Why do many time-series programs start by taking the logarithm of the series?

choices.text: To remove the trend
choices.why: A log changes the scale, not the direction: a rising series still rises.

choices.text: A log turns products into sums
choices.why: Right. The log of a product is a sum, and the answers are turned back with exp.

choices.text: Logs make every series stationary
choices.why: A log alone removes neither trend nor season.

choices.text: To keep big numbers from overflowing
choices.why: A few thousand orders is nowhere near any limit.

prompt: An additive decomposition is fitted to Panela's daily orders. What will its residuals show?

choices.text: A weekly ripple, opposite in sign at the two ends of the data
choices.why: Right. One average gap is too big for 2023 and too small for 2025.

choices.text: Nothing unusual, because additive and multiplicative agree on average
choices.why: They agree in the middle of the data and disagree at both ends, and the residuals show where.

choices.text: A slow drift upwards
choices.why: The trend is fitted either way; the error is in the size of the season.

choices.text: Larger residuals on holidays only
choices.why: Holidays are large residuals under either model.

prompt: A classical decomposition of weekly data with period=52 leaves how many weeks without a trend at each end?
The seasonal index of the first week of the year is 0.812. What does it mean?

choices.text: That week takes 812 orders fewer than the trend
choices.why: That would be an additive index in orders. This one is a multiplier.

choices.text: 81.2 per cent of the orders of that year fall in that week
choices.why: An index compares a week with the trend, not with the year's total.

choices.text: The first week of next year will be 0.812 times this one
choices.why: The index compares a week with the trend at that time, not one year with the next.

choices.text: That week takes about 19 per cent fewer orders than the trend
choices.why: Right. In a multiplicative model the index multiplies the trend.

prompt: Panela raised prices in September 2025. Why does the classical trend, computed on weeks up to December 2025, show nothing of it?

choices.text: The rise was too small to show in a trend
choices.why: Monthly orders fell by about a seventh. The trend simply has no values there.

choices.text: The rise was absorbed into the seasonal index
choices.why: In the classical method the season is averaged over years where the trend exists, so it never saw those weeks either.

choices.text: It stops in June, half a year before the data ends
choices.why: Right. A centred 52-week window cannot reach the last half-year.

choices.text: A multiplicative model cannot represent a fall
choices.why: A multiplier below the previous level is a fall like any other.

prompt: Which of these are steps of the classical multiplicative decomposition? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: A centred moving average as long as the period, to estimate the trend
choices.why: Right. That is step one.

choices.text: Averaging the series divided by the trend over each position of the season
choices.why: Right. That is step two, and it gives the seasonal index.

choices.text: Fitting a regression around each point
choices.why: That is loess, which STL uses instead of moving averages.

choices.text: Re-weighting weeks that look like outliers
choices.why: That is STL's robust option; the classical method has none.

prompt: Carnival fell in a February week in 2024 and a March week in 2025. In the residuals of a classical decomposition, what does that leave?

choices.text: Nothing: averaging the same week over several years removes a holiday that moves
choices.why: It does not remove it, it smears it, and the residual is where the smear shows.

choices.text: A low and a high in a pair of weeks
choices.why: Right. The index averaged half a Carnival into each of those weeks.

choices.text: One low residual, in the 2025 week only
choices.why: The 2024 week and the weeks without Carnival are mis-explained too.

choices.text: A drift in the trend
choices.why: A few weeks are far too short to move a 52-week average.

prompt: A residual series sits above 1 for five months and then below 1 for five months. What does that suggest?

choices.text: The trend was too stiff
choices.why: Right. Residuals that drift are a level the trend did not follow.

choices.text: A missed weekly season
choices.why: A missed weekly season shows as a ripple every week, not a months-long drift.

choices.text: Ordinary noise, which can run in long streaks
choices.why: Noise has no memory, so it does not run for months on one side of 1.

choices.text: A holiday
choices.why: A holiday is a few days, not five months.

prompt: Put the three questions for reading a residual series in the order the lesson asks them.
items: Where are the largest values, and do they have names?

prompt: What does STL do that the classical decomposition cannot?

choices.text: Work without choosing a period
choices.why: STL needs the period too: period=52 in the lesson.

choices.text: Handle a multiplicative series without a logarithm, since it multiplies its components internally
choices.why: STL adds, which is why the lesson gives it np.log of the series.

choices.text: Forecast the next year
choices.why: A decomposition describes the past; forecasting is lessons 3 and 4.

choices.text: Produce a trend for the first and last weeks of the data
choices.why: Right. A regression can be fitted at the edge, a centred average cannot.

prompt: The latest value of an STL trend is the one every manager reads. Why should it be trusted least?

choices.text: Loess is less accurate on recent data
choices.why: Recency is not the problem; having neighbours on only one side is.

choices.text: The robust option ignores the last weeks
choices.why: Robust weights depend on how badly a week is explained, not on where it sits.

choices.text: Its neighbours are all on one side
choices.why: Right. The edge of a smoother is always provisional.

choices.text: It should not: the last value has the most data behind it
choices.why: It has the most data before it and none after, and a centre needs both.

prompt: What does robust=True change in STL?

choices.text: It uses medians instead of means
choices.why: It keeps loess; what changes is the weight each week gets.

choices.text: It refits, giving less weight to the weeks it explained worst
choices.why: Right. One strange week then pulls the fit less.

choices.text: It makes the season identical every year
choices.why: That is the seasonal smoothing setting, a different choice.

choices.text: It lets the trend reach the ends
choices.why: STL reaches the ends with or without it.

prompt: A week took 10,804 orders and its seasonal index is 1.104. What is its seasonally adjusted value, to the nearest order?
Orders fell 30 per cent from the week before Christmas to the first week of January, and the seasonally adjusted value barely moved. What happened in January?

choices.text: Nothing unusual: the fall was the season
choices.why: Right. Season aside, January was an ordinary month.

choices.text: Customers left after the holidays
choices.why: If they had, the adjusted value would have fallen too.

choices.text: The adjustment hid a real fall
choices.why: The adjustment removes only what happens in that week every year.

choices.text: The trend turned down
choices.why: An adjusted value that holds steady says the opposite.

prompt: What is the difference between the trend and the seasonally adjusted series?

choices.text: None; they are two names for one series
choices.why: They differ by the noise, which is exactly why one wobbles and the other does not.

choices.text: The trend still carries the season, since only the noise was averaged out of it
choices.why: The trend carries neither season nor noise.

choices.text: The adjusted series is smoother
choices.why: It is rougher, because the noise is still in it.

choices.text: Only one keeps the noise: the adjusted series
choices.why: Right. Only the season is removed from it.

prompt: Match each piece of a multiplicative decomposition to how it is obtained.

pairs.right: a centred moving average as long as the period
the series over the trend, averaged per position
the series over trend and season
the series over the season alone

prompt: STL replaces moving averages with ___, a smoother that fits a small weighted regression around each point.
A sales director compares this December with this November and celebrates a 9 per cent rise. Which series should the comparison use?

choices.text: The trend, because it removes everything but direction
choices.why: The trend of a classical decomposition has no value for the last months, which are these two.

choices.text: The raw series, since 9 per cent is a real rise in orders
choices.why: It is real and it is mostly season: December beats November every year.

choices.text: The seasonally adjusted series
choices.why: Right. December is always busier than November; adjusted, the two are comparable.

choices.text: The residual
choices.why: The residual removes the trend as well, and the director's question is partly about it.

prompt: A centred seven-day moving average has no value for how many days at the end of a series?
